chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
title: Max Roach and Kenny Clarke, the younger drummers
summary: Moore considers Max Roach the top bop drummer, never copying anyone, and met him around 1929 by his reckoning.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Okay, then that was that same session. Now, up until this time, of course, there's a new type of music in Jazz that is on the scene, with some younger musicians, and they had their special way of playing the drums, and there were drummers like Kenny Clarke and Max Roach, among others. Did you get an opportunity to hear these younger drummers? And what was your reaction to them? What did you think of them?

Well, I didn't get the opportunity to meet too many of the younger drummers. Like Kenny Clarke, he was a very good drummer. And there was a drummer who was living over... I think he passed away. He was in Paris there for a while. But he wasn't necessarily a younger drummer; but he had a lot of experience. It will come to me after a while, what that boy's name is over in Paris, France. He had just come out of the Army.

Well, a lot of the... Max Roach and Kenny Clarke are two of the drummers who, being involved with the music of, say, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Come, also paid a great deal of respect to Big Sid Catlett. Had you heard about this new musical style from the musicians who might get together and just have your (?) sessions, or you'd be talking about music and musicians? Did you talk about what
Moore (III) - 54

the drummers were doing or what they were not doing? Say, Dizzy Come... You were playing music before Dizzy was born or before Charlie Parker was born. So they were coming in, it seemed, with a new sound. Did much of that impress you in any way, or was it something that didn't really...it wasn't very important to you?
One of the main drummers who used to play with Dizzy, that drummer I just mentioned a while ago...
Kenny Clarke?
No, that other one.
Max Roach?
Yeah. Now, he was the top drummer for all that. He was the top drummer, Max Roach. He's still living, ain't he?
Oh yes.
He's still drumming, too, isn't he?
Yes, he is.

But he knows all the roots; he knows how to play all of that different stuff. But most of the drummers (?) listen to other drummers and copy them, what they play. But Max Roach never did copy nobody. That's his style of playing.
That's the way he does it.
Moore (III) - 55

And Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, a lot of them -- well, he could back them up. Knew how to play on different things, tom-toms, whatever it is -- he knew how. He was a great drummer. Of course, I didn't put no other drummers down. But I mean, I know about him! In that style.
And he impressed you early on.
Yeah. Because that style of playing.
Did you ever have a chance to talk with him?
Oh yeah, we sat down and talked. He taken a liking to me right away, you know. I met him around 1929, around there, sometime there...
Yeah.
I think he was a boy in short pants at that time. Max Roach, he's...
Somewhere around there I met him!
Yeah? He was a child.
Oh yeah?

Max Roach, let's see... I think it would have 1949, yeah. Because he was a young man then, and he was playing with people like Miles Davis and Charlie Parker and some of the other musicians, I believe Lucky Thompson and so forth.
